source.title: Can Neural Network Memorization Be Localized?
source.authors: Pratyush Maini; M. Mozer; Hanie Sedghi; Zachary Chase Lipton; J. Kolter; Chiyuan Zhang

record.file_problem: Full paper text, including appendix, is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests memorization on randomly mislabeled examples and compares standard dropout with an example-tied dropout method, but its central experiments localize memorization using gradient accounting, layer rewinding/retraining, and neuron removal rather than reproducing the original all-random-label experiment.
record.gate_note: The paper cites prior work on random-label memorization in its Introduction; those cited results are not recorded as this study's results. Its own relevant results use datasets with 10% random label noise, plus a standard-dropout baseline. Example-tied dropout results are not evidence that an unmodified standard network fits labels, since the method changes training.
record.test_reason: Standard SGD training and clean-versus-noisy training-accuracy curves directly test V6; the standard-dropout baseline tests the dropout component of V5. The localization experiments address a separate question. No experiment establishes fitting a completely randomly labeled training set as specified by V1.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: memorization is not generally confined to the last or a few layers, individual memorized predictions often depend on a small set of neurons distributed across layers, and example-tied dropout can direct memorization toward predetermined neurons.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses 10% randomly mislabeled subsets and examines where memorization is represented; it does not reproduce the original fully randomized-label experiment. It also introduces example-tied dropout, a training modification.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that critical layers differ by model architecture and dataset; its example-tied-dropout localization outcome varies with pgen and pmem.

fits_no_version.finding: Example-tied dropout achieves 99.9% clean and 99.3% noisy training accuracy before removing designated memorization neurons.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training with example-specific neuron assignments can fit a randomly mislabeled subset.

fits_no_version.finding: Layer rewinding, retraining, and neuron removal indicate distributed layer involvement and concentrated neuron-level sensitivity of memorized predictions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Memorized predictions depend on small neuron subsets distributed across layers.

fits_no_version.finding: Noisy examples contribute substantial, oppositely directed gradients throughout training, including before their labels are fitted.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Noisy examples influence optimization throughout training even when their prediction accuracy improves later.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning, Proceedings of Machine Learning Research 202, 2023
record.problems: The central results generally concern a 10% mislabeled subset rather than fully random labels. Several learning-curve and layer-rewinding outcomes are provided only in figures. ResNet gradient-accounting and weight-rewinding results are averaged over 3 seeds; ViT results are excepted from that averaging statement.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-bearing rows omitted. Figure-only layer-rewinding results are not extracted because they do not measure a version's named outcome more directly than the reported training-accuracy and learning-curve rows.

untested.parts: Completely random labeling, near-zero error on that entire training set, chance test performance, and unchanged architecture and hyperparameters relative to true-label training.
Training-time ratios against true-label fitting and convergence slowdown across corruption fractions.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training fit together with steadily worsening test error across a zero-to-all corruption sweep. The gradient-norm sweep does not measure these outcomes.
Weight decay, data augmentation, dropout under completely random labeling, and generalization on true labels after removing explicit regularization.
Learning dynamics under fully random labeling; the directly recorded trajectory concerns a 10% mislabeled subset.

missing.what: Separate clean-versus-noisy training trajectories for ResNet-50 and ViT-small are shown but omitted from the rows. Extract their qualitative learning order and final fitting levels from the original plots before assigning model-specific verdicts; the supplied text transcription does not preserve the curves.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source for these versions. Corruption assigns an incorrect class at random, rather than independently drawing from all classes. Untested conditions do not warrant limits_scope labels. Example-tied-dropout removal results do not challenge V5's statement about standard regularization.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests randomly mislabeled subsets, usually at 10% noise, not a completely random labeling of the whole training set. It does not establish test error at chance for an all-random labeling or compare unchanged training hyperparameters against true-label training.
No small-constant-factor training-time comparison or convergence-time sweep over corrupted-label fractions is reported.
No shuffled-pixel, permuted-pixel, or Gaussian-noise input fitting experiment is reported.
Although gradient contributions are examined across noise rates, the study does not report training and test error across a zero-to-all label-noise sweep.

The study compares standard dropout with a sparse network and an example-tied dropout method on noisy training labels. It does not test weight decay or data augmentation, nor whether removing regularization alone harms true-label generalization.

Learning curves for clean and mislabeled examples are shown in Figure 3, and the text says noisy-example accuracy stays below 20% until epoch 30. Exact per-epoch values are figure-only; the paper does not establish the broader claim for fully random labels.
